title: Combating Misinformation in the Age of LLMs: Opportunities and Challenges
extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of research on combating misinformation in the age of large language models (LLMs). It asks two broad questions: how LLMs can be used to detect, intervene in, and attribute misinformation, and how to counter misinformation generated by LLMs themselves. The paper situates LLMs as a double-edged technology: they can help fact-checking because of their world knowledge, reasoning ability, and ability to use tools or external knowledge, but they can also generate deceptive content at scale.

The paper does not study a classroom, school, or K-12 intervention. Instead, it reviews prior work on misinformation detection methods before LLMs and then summarizes emerging work using LLMs for misinformation detection, multimodal misinformation, and fact-checking assistance. It also discusses broader opportunities such as misinformation intervention, attribution, and human-LLM collaboration, and highlights risks such as hallucinations, malicious content generation, and autonomous misinformation agents.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial promise for supporting misinformation detection and response, but they also introduce new harms that require technical, social, educational, and policy countermeasures. The paper argues for stronger factuality and safety controls, better detection of LLM-generated misinformation, and interdisciplinary efforts to protect information ecosystems. Because it is a survey and position paper, it provides no direct empirical evidence about K-12 science inquiry supports, student populations, or classroom outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey paper about LLMs, misinformation detection, and safety rather than an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention. It does not present a study design, sample, or measured learner outcomes relevant to K-12 evidence grading.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact on student learning or school outcomes. Its relevance is conceptual and methodological for misinformation and AI safety, not an evaluated educational intervention with observable effect sizes.
